claims.claim: By the best cell counts we have, a typical man is about half human.
claims.source_checked: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC4991899/fullTextXML (Sender, Fuchs & Milo, PLoS Biol 14(8): e1002533, 2016, doi:10.1371/journal.pbio.1002533, full text incl. Tables 1-3); https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC10523466/fullTextXML (Hatton et al., PNAS 120(39): e2303077120, 2023, doi:10.1073/pnas.2303077120)
claims.note: Sender: 'the typical adult human body consists of about 30 trillion human cells and about 38 trillion bacteria' (70 kg 'reference man'); 30/68 = 44%. Hatton: '≈36 trillion cells in the male' (70 kg) and it cites Sender for 'an approximately equal number of bacteria cells'; 36/74 = 49%. 'About half' holds on both. 'Typical' is Sender's own word. 'Best cell counts we have' is framing: Hatton (2023) is the most recent whole-body human census, and it uses Sender (2016) for bacteria, which is still the reference bacterial count it cites. 'By ... cell counts' limits the claim to counts, not mass or genes. Holds for the man only: Sender's reference woman is 21 vs 44 trillion (32%), and the line says 'man'.

claims.claim: Hook as seen by a viewer who swipes away at 2.0 s: voice 'By the best cell counts we have,' (word 'a' starts at 1.962 s, 'typical' at 2.176 s); captions already show the whole first sentence ('...A TYPICAL MAN IS ABOUT HALF HUMAN.'), upcoming words greyed; Lab shows 68 identical dots in a human shape; Cutout shows the Vitruvian Man and 'BY CELL COUNT'.
claims.where: spoken + on-screen: hook at second two (A4)
claims.source_checked: src/generated/cell-count.alignment.json word timings (words match the script text exactly); stills rendered with `npx remotion still` at frame 60 of cell-count-Lab and cell-count-cutout-Cutout; https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC4991899/fullTextXML (Sender, Fuchs & Milo, PLoS Biol 14(8): e1002533, 2016, doi:10.1371/journal.pbio.1002533, full text incl. Tables 1-3)
claims.note: Nothing false is shown or said by 2 s. The take-away a swiper can read (a typical man is about half human by cell count) is the corrected form of the popular '10% human / 10 bacteria for every human cell' myth, which Sender says 'should replace the 10:1 or 100:1 values that are stated in the literature'. The short does not claim bacteria outnumber human cells, so a swiper is not left with the popular falsehood.

claims.note: 'Reference Man is defined as being between 20–30 years of age, weighing 70 kg, is 170 cm in height'; 'calculated 2% uncertainty and 14% CV. We note that the uncertainty and CV estimates might be too optimistically low'; 'B/H = 1.3, with an uncertainty of 25%'; 'This B/H value of about 1:1'.

claims.claim: Sender is 'the only one [of the two] that pairs human cells and bacteria for the same reference body'
claims.source_checked: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC10523466/fullTextXML (Hatton et al., PNAS 120(39): e2303077120, 2023, doi:10.1073/pnas.2303077120)
claims.note: Hatton does not estimate bacteria. It cites Sender (ref 17) for 'an approximately equal number of bacteria cells', and its Fig 3 marks 'the bacterial microbiome (17)'.

claims.claim: Hatton: '≈36 trillion cells in the male' (70 kg, 176 cm, 20-50 y), '≈28 trillion in the female'; earlier studies 'converging on values of 30 to 37 trillion human cells'; cites Sender for 'an approximately equal number of bacteria cells'
claims.source_checked: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC10523466/fullTextXML (Hatton et al., PNAS 120(39): e2303077120, 2023, doi:10.1073/pnas.2303077120); Hatton et al. Dataset S01 (pnas.2303077120.sd01.xlsx, from https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC10523466/supplementaryFiles), sheet Master_Cell_Data summed per body
claims.note: All quotations are verbatim. 'Male, (70 kg, 176 cm in height and 20 to 50 y of age)'. Dataset S1 Tissue_Table gives the same 70 kg / 176 cm / 20-50. Summed Master_Cell_Data: 36.49 and 27.82 trillion.

claims.claim: '30 of 68 trillion is 44% human (Sender), 36 of 74 is 49% (Hatton with Sender's bacteria)'
claims.source_checked: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC4991899/fullTextXML (Sender, Fuchs & Milo, PLoS Biol 14(8): e1002533, 2016, doi:10.1371/journal.pbio.1002533, full text incl. Tables 1-3); https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC10523466/fullTextXML (Hatton et al., PNAS 120(39): e2303077120, 2023, doi:10.1073/pnas.2303077120)

claims.claim: 'Sender's reference woman is about a third human (21 and 44 trillion)', 'its other groups 30-42%'
claims.source_checked: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC4991899/fullTextXML (Sender, Fuchs & Milo, PLoS Biol 14(8): e1002533, 2016, doi:10.1371/journal.pbio.1002533, full text incl. Tables 1-3)
claims.note: Table 3: ref. woman 21 human / 44 bacteria (32%), B:H 2.2. Young infant 1.9/4.4 (30%), infant 4/7 (36%), elder 22/38 (37%), obese 40/56 (42%).

claims.claim: Hatton's three bodies have red cells at 73%, 71%, 71%; 'Sender measures 84% for the reference man and assumes it for its other groups'
claims.source_checked: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC4991899/fullTextXML (Sender, Fuchs & Milo, PLoS Biol 14(8): e1002533, 2016, doi:10.1371/journal.pbio.1002533, full text incl. Tables 1-3); Hatton et al. Dataset S01 (pnas.2303077120.sd01.xlsx, from https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC10523466/supplementaryFiles), sheet Master_Cell_Data summed per body
claims.note: Dataset S1 (erythrocyte rows): 72.7%, 71.0%, 71.0%. Sender Table 3 note (2): 'Assuming RBCs account for 84% of the total host cells as observed for the reference man.' Sender's 84% is a calculated estimate ('observed'), not a measurement, so 'estimates' would be the more exact word than 'measures'. This is internal wording only, and no change is required.

claims.claim: Nucleated-only comparison gives about 10:1 ('a question of definition'); microbial cells 'operationally' called bacteria; archaea and eukaryotes 2-3 orders of magnitude fewer
claims.source_checked: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC4991899/fullTextXML (Sender, Fuchs & Milo, PLoS Biol 14(8): e1002533, 2016, doi:10.1371/journal.pbio.1002533, full text incl. Tables 1-3)
claims.note: 'if one chooses to compare the number of bacteria ... to the number of nucleated human cells (≈0.3·10^13), the ratio will be about 10:1'; 'seems to be a question of definition'; 'We therefore sometimes operationally refer to the microbial cells in the human body as bacteria'; 'Bacteria overwhelmingly outnumber eukaryotes and archaea ... by 2–3 orders of magnitude'.

claims.claim: Bacteria 'nearly all in the colon'; colon estimate 'in some respects ... an upper limit'
claims.source_checked: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC4991899/fullTextXML (Sender, Fuchs & Milo, PLoS Biol 14(8): e1002533, 2016, doi:10.1371/journal.pbio.1002533, full text incl. Tables 1-3)
claims.note: 'The vast majority of the bacteria reside in the colon'; other organs contribute 'at most 10^12'; 'In some respects, the estimate we performed of multiplying observed fecal bacteria density with colon content volume can be considered an upper limit.'

claims.claim: Bacterial mass ~0.2 kg; Sender revises earlier 1-3 kg (1-3% of body mass), citing an NIH news release (ref. 25)
claims.source_checked: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC4991899/fullTextXML (Sender, Fuchs & Milo, PLoS Biol 14(8): e1002533, 2016, doi:10.1371/journal.pbio.1002533, full text incl. Tables 1-3)
claims.note: 'significantly updating previous statements that 1%–3% of the body mass is composed of bacteria or that a normal human hosts 1–3 kg of bacteria [25]'. Ref 25 is the 'NIH Human Microbiome Project defines normal bacterial makeup of the body' news release (2012).

claims.claim: Sender 'The cell count is dominated by red blood cells (84%)', 2.5e13 of 3.0e13; Hatton non-nucleated blood cells ≈29 of ≈36 trillion; Dataset S1 red cells ≈26.5 of 36.5 (man), 19.8 of 27.8 (woman)
